h1: What Size Extra Virgin Olive Oil Bottle Should You Buy?
excerpt: Choosing between 250 ml, 500 ml and a tin is arithmetic, not taste: how fast your kitchen empties a bottle, held against the roughly two months an opened bottle stays at its best.
keyTakeaway: Buy the size your kitchen finishes inside roughly two months of opening, because that is how long an opened bottle holds its character. Count the pours in a normal week, multiply by fifteen millilitres, and let the answer pick the bottle. A large tin is only cheaper per litre if the last pour is still good.
heroAlt: A bottling line with olive oil running from stainless steel filling heads into a row of dark glass bottles standing in line on a conveyor.
inlineAlt: Dark glass olive oil bottles moving along a filling line under stainless steel filling heads
intro: A shelf holding a 250 ml bottle, a 500 ml bottle and a three-litre tin is a maths problem dressed up as a taste test. The lowest price per litre is worth nothing if the last third goes flat before anyone pours it.
Measure how fast your kitchen empties a bottle against the roughly two months an opened one stays at its best, and the size chooses itself.

sections.heading: Start by counting the pours in a normal week

blocks.text: A tablespoon is about 15 ml, which turns a vague habit into a number. A kitchen that only dresses salads pours roughly 30 ml a week and takes eight weeks to empty 250 ml. A kitchen that fries, roasts and dresses with olive oil clears 500 ml inside a month.

items: **One tablespoon** is about 15 ml, so three a week is 45 ml.
**Salads and finishing only:** roughly 30 ml a week.
**Cooking with it most days:** 100 ml a week and up.

blocks.text: Match the bottle to a household's weekly pour and to the eight-week window, not to the shelf price. Any row where the bottle outlasts eight weeks is a row where the smaller size is the better buy, whatever the label says per litre.

sections.heading: Why the big tin is only cheaper if you finish it

blocks.text: A three-litre tin advertises a price per litre that assumes every millilitre is used while it is still good. Open it in a kitchen that pours 100 ml a week and the tin has thirty weeks to give against a bottle that keeps its character for eight.
A tin also breathes. Every pour draws air into the space above the oil, and a tin two-thirds empty is mostly air. Tins suit a restaurant that empties one in a fortnight.

sections.heading: Decanting a tin into a smaller dark bottle

blocks.text: Decanting is what makes a tin work at home: the bulk stays sealed and dark while a small bottle does the daily pouring. It costs nothing but a clean bottle and five minutes, and it is the only reason a large format belongs in a two-person kitchen.

items: Wash a small dark glass bottle and dry it completely before it sees oil.
Fill it to the shoulder, not halfway, so little air sits above the oil.
Reseal the tin at once and keep it in a cupboard away from the stove.
Empty and dry the small bottle before refilling. Never top fresh oil onto old.

sections.heading: What to check on the bottle itself

blocks.text: The container is part of what you are buying. Dark glass and tin both keep light off the oil; a clear bottle under retail lighting ages fastest. Read the harvest date before the best-before date, and check the grade is printed in words, not implied by a picture.

items: **Dark glass or tin.** Clear bottles sit under shop lights for months.
**A harvest date.** The age of the oil, not of the packing run.
**The grade written out.** Extra virgin, in words, on the front.
**A cap that reseals cleanly.** A pourer that will not close leaks air.

sections.heading: When the larger bottle is the right call

blocks.text: Buy the larger bottle when the kitchen genuinely empties it inside two months, which happens more often than people assume once olive oil replaces the everyday cooking oil rather than sitting beside it. Roasting vegetables twice a week accounts for much of 500 ml.

Buying two small bottles and opening the second only when the first is done also works. Sealed stock ages slowly, as [olive oil shelf life](/blog/olive-oil-shelf-life-how-long-a-bottle-lasts) sets out.
Count the pours, multiply by 15 ml, and pick the bottle your kitchen empties within about two months of opening. Buy a tin only if you decant into a small dark bottle.

faqs.q: Is a 250 ml or a 500 ml olive oil bottle better?
faqs.a: Whichever one your kitchen finishes within about two months. A household that only dresses salads takes eight weeks over 250 ml. One cooking with olive oil most days empties 500 ml in about five weeks.

faqs.q: How much olive oil does a family of four use in a month?
faqs.a: A family using olive oil as the main cooking oil pours somewhere near 225 ml a week, so close to a litre a month. A family reserving it for salads and finishing may take two months over 250 ml.

faqs.q: Is buying a large tin of olive oil cheaper?
faqs.a: Per litre, yes. In practice it is only cheaper if the last pour is still good. A tin that takes a household six months to empty has spent four of those months past its best.

faqs.q: Can I decant olive oil into a smaller bottle?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the sensible way to use a tin at home. Use a clean, completely dry dark glass bottle, fill it near the shoulder to limit air, and reseal the tin straight after pouring.

faqs.q: Why is olive oil sold in dark glass bottles?
faqs.a: Light drives the reaction that flattens an oil's fruit and pepper, so dark glass and tin both slow it. A clear bottle standing under shop lighting for months ages faster than the same oil in green glass.

faqs.q: What size bottle suits one person living alone?
faqs.a: The smallest one sold. A single household drizzling olive oil now and then pours perhaps a tablespoon a week, and even 250 ml at that rate outlasts the window where the oil is at its best.
